---
title: "Our approach"
description: "Where urban climate learning can break down and how the four questions connect."
---

<p class="page-deck">Cities often talk about moving from evidence to action. The path is rarely that simple. Research can be hard to find, poorly matched to local circumstances or interpreted differently by the people making a decision. A policy may then stall in delivery, or an assessment may overlook its wider effects.</p>

The lab studies how people produce, compare, use and revise urban climate knowledge. We ask how cities can make better-grounded decisions without assuming that evidence applies unchanged across places.

<p class="term-first-use">How a policy's costs, benefits and wider effects are assessed is its <strong>appraisal</strong>. The data, institutions and tools through which evidence is produced and used form its <strong>evidence infrastructure</strong>.</p>

## Illustration: expanding active travel {#illustration-expanding-active-travel}

::: {.notice}
**Hypothetical illustration.** This is a hypothetical illustration of the four questions, not a finding or policy recommendation.
:::

<ol class="cycle-illustration">
  <li><strong>Relevance across places.</strong> City staff examine evidence from elsewhere, but travel patterns, street rules or climate may change the lesson.</li>
  <li><strong>New evidence.</strong> Researchers might learn more by studying local uptake or distribution than by adding another general case study.</li>
  <li><strong>Delivery.</strong> Transport agencies, local government and communities have to organise authority, funding, maintenance and participation.</li>
  <li><strong>Consequences and further learning.</strong> Different residents could experience changes in health, access, safety or affordability. Those results would shape what cities learn next.</li>
</ol>

## Where urban climate learning can break down

These six states show why a linear sequence is too simple. They mark places where the four-theme learning cycle can break down, not a second framework or a universal sequence.

<ol class="approach-states">
  <li><strong>People produce evidence and make it visible.</strong> Researchers, public agencies, professionals, communities and Indigenous knowledge holders need routes through which their knowledge can reach a decision.</li>
  <li><strong>Decision-makers judge relevance.</strong> A well-known or nearby example may still be a poor guide if the important local conditions differ.</li>
  <li><strong>Researchers choose new evidence for what it could change.</strong> Missing knowledge matters most when resolving it could alter how a policy is assessed, distinguish between explanations or expand who can learn.</li>
  <li><strong>People interpret evidence and organise delivery.</strong> Public officials, utilities, community organisations and others bring different judgement, authority, resources and capabilities to the work.</li>
  <li><strong>Communities experience consequences.</strong> Benefits, burdens, risks and unintended effects fall across different people, places and periods. How a policy's costs, benefits and wider effects are assessed—its <strong>appraisal</strong>—determines which effects count.</li>
  <li><strong>People use the results to revise later decisions.</strong> Outcomes expose unanswered questions, test prior assumptions and change what another place might learn.</li>
</ol>

## Commitments

- Contextual relevance should be examined rather than assumed.
- Evidence status and uncertainty should remain visible.
- A case may be useful without providing a universally transferable model.
- Failures and partial implementation may provide valuable knowledge.
- Local, professional, administrative, community and Indigenous knowledge should not be treated merely as inferior substitutes for published research.
- Questions about whose knowledge travels and whose outcomes are counted are questions of authority and justice.
- The lab does not seek context-free lists of universal best practices.
